threatContext.stream-hijacking: Consumer group hijacking by joining existing consumer groups with stolen credentials, topic partition reassignment manipulation, rogue consumer registration intercepting messages before legitimate consumers, producer impersonation injecting false records into topics
threatContext.unauthorized-access: Broker authentication bypass via misconfigured SASL/SCRAM or mTLS settings, ZooKeeper (legacy) or KRaft controller access without authentication, topic ACL misconfiguration granting wildcard access, MSK Connect worker accessing unauthorized topics, unauthenticated bootstrap server connections
threatContext.data-exfiltration: Bulk topic consumption via kafka-console-consumer with stolen credentials, MSK Connect sink connector redirecting data to attacker-controlled destinations, cross-account cluster replication abuse, topic mirroring to external Kafka clusters via MirrorMaker
threatContext.misconfiguration: Topic ACLs allowing wildcard (*) produce/consume on all topics, PLAINTEXT listeners enabled alongside SASL/TLS, auto.create.topics.enable allowing unauthorized topic creation, missing encryption in transit between brokers (inter-broker TLS disabled), default replication factor of 1 risking data loss, MSK Serverless VPC endpoint policies too permissive, Schema Registry without authentication exposing schema definitions
threatContext.sensitive-data-exposure: Unencrypted message payloads containing PII flowing through topics, Schema Registry exposing data structure and field names, broker logs capturing message metadata, Connect worker configurations containing database credentials in plaintext, consumer lag metrics revealing data processing patterns
threatContext.credential-theft: SASL/SCRAM credentials extracted from AWS Secrets Manager via IAM policy abuse, mTLS client certificates stolen from poorly secured keystores, MSK Connect worker credential exposure in connector configurations, bootstrap broker credentials in application configuration files, IAM access credentials for MSK Serverless authentication
threatContext.message-tampering: Malicious producer injecting corrupted or falsified records into topics, Schema Registry poisoning by registering incompatible or malicious schemas causing consumer deserialization failures, idempotent producer ID spoofing, transaction coordinator manipulation causing duplicate or out-of-order message delivery
threatContext.dos-attack: Broker resource exhaustion via large message production exceeding max.message.bytes, partition count explosion through automated topic creation, consumer group rebalance storms caused by rapid join/leave cycles, uncompressed message flooding consuming broker disk and network, ZooKeeper/KRaft session flooding disrupting cluster coordination

stream-hijacking: Enforce SASL/SCRAM or IAM authentication on all broker listeners to prevent unauthorized consumer group joins
Configure Kafka ACLs to restrict consumer group IDs to specific authenticated principals
Enable MSK cluster logging to CloudWatch to detect unauthorized consumer registrations and partition reassignments
Use dedicated consumer groups per application with unique group.id values and ACL enforcement
unauthorized-access: Enable IAM access control or SASL/SCRAM authentication and disable PLAINTEXT listeners entirely
Configure Kafka ACLs with deny-by-default and grant produce/consume permissions per topic per principal
Restrict MSK cluster security groups to specific client CIDR ranges and VPC subnets
Use MSK Serverless with IAM authentication to eliminate broker-level credential management
data-exfiltration: Restrict Kafka ACLs to prevent unauthorized topic consumption using per-topic, per-principal permissions
Configure MSK Connect sink connectors with IAM roles scoped to specific destination resource ARNs only
Enable encryption in transit (TLS) for all client-broker and inter-broker communication
Use VPC endpoints and private subnets to ensure broker traffic never traverses the public internet
misconfiguration: Disable auto.create.topics.enable in broker configuration to prevent unauthorized topic creation
Enforce TLS encryption in transit for both client-broker and inter-broker communication
Set minimum.insync.replicas and default replication factor to at least 2 for data durability
Use AWS Config rules to detect MSK clusters without encryption at rest or missing authentication
sensitive-data-exposure: Enable encryption at rest using customer-managed KMS keys on all MSK clusters
Enforce TLS encryption in transit to protect message payloads containing sensitive data
Store MSK Connect worker credentials in Secrets Manager instead of plaintext connector configurations
Restrict access to MSK broker logs and CloudWatch log groups containing message metadata
credential-theft: Restrict Secrets Manager access for SASL/SCRAM credentials using IAM policies scoped to specific secret ARNs
Use IAM access control for MSK Serverless to eliminate static SASL/SCRAM credentials entirely
Store mTLS client certificates and keystores in AWS Certificate Manager or Secrets Manager with rotation enabled
Enforce least-privilege IAM policies for kafka-cluster:Connect and kafka-cluster:ReadData actions
message-tampering: Enable idempotent producers and configure Kafka ACLs to restrict IdempotentWrite to authorized producer principals
Enforce Schema Registry compatibility checks (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) to prevent malicious schema registration
Restrict Kafka ACLs for producer write access on a per-topic basis to authorized principals only
Enable transactional producers with ACLs restricting TransactionalId usage to specific authenticated applications
dos-attack: Configure broker-level quotas (producer_byte_rate, consumer_byte_rate) to limit per-client throughput
Set max.message.bytes and message.max.bytes to reject oversized messages at the broker level
Disable auto.create.topics.enable and restrict CreateTopics ACL to prevent partition count explosion
Configure MSK cluster scaling and CloudWatch alarms for broker CPU, disk, and network utilization

services.name: Simple Email Service
services.description: Managed email sending and receiving service for transactional and marketing emails

threatContext.injection-attack: Email header injection via unsanitized From/To/Subject fields, HTML/JavaScript injection in email body templates, SMTP command injection through raw SendRawEmail API
threatContext.credential-theft: SMTP credential theft (IAM-derived SMTP username/password), SES API access key exposure, compromised sending authorization delegate credentials
threatContext.sensitive-data-exposure: PII in email bodies and attachments sent via SES, bounce/complaint notifications containing recipient data, email content logged in CloudWatch or S3 configuration sets
threatContext.account-takeover: Compromised SES SMTP credentials used for spam/phishing campaigns, domain spoofing via missing SPF/DKIM/DMARC, sending authorization abuse from delegate accounts
threatContext.data-exfiltration: Bulk email address harvesting from SES suppression list, email content exfiltration via S3 receipt rule actions, redirect of received emails to attacker-controlled destinations

misconfiguration: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for all verified sending domains to prevent spoofing
Enable SES configuration sets with event publishing to monitor bounce, complaint, and delivery metrics
Move SES out of sandbox mode only for production accounts and restrict sending quotas to expected volumes
Use AWS Config rules to detect SES identities without DKIM signing enabled
sensitive-data-exposure: Encrypt email content at rest using customer-managed KMS keys for S3 receipt rule storage
Avoid including sensitive PII directly in email bodies; use secure links or tokenized references instead
Restrict access to SES event destination S3 buckets and CloudWatch log groups containing email metadata
Configure SES virtual deliverability manager to monitor sending reputation without exposing content
unauthorized-access: Restrict ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail IAM permissions to specific verified identity ARNs
Use SES sending authorization policies to control which delegates can send on behalf of your identities
Enforce aws:SourceVpc conditions on SES IAM policies to restrict API access to trusted networks
Enable CloudTrail data events for SES to audit all email sending and configuration API calls
injection-attack: Use the SES v2 SendEmail API with structured message parameters instead of SendRawEmail for application-generated emails
Validate and sanitize all user-supplied input before including it in email headers or body content
Use SES email templates with parameterized variables to prevent injection through template rendering
credential-theft: Use IAM roles for SES API access instead of generating long-lived SMTP credentials
Store SES SMTP credentials in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation instead of application configuration files
Restrict SES SMTP credential usage to specific IP ranges using IAM policy conditions
account-takeover: Configure DMARC with a reject policy (p=reject) and monitor aggregate/forensic reports for unauthorized sending
Enable SES account-level suppression list to automatically stop sending to addresses that bounce or complain
Use dedicated SES sending identities per application to isolate reputation and limit blast radius of compromise
data-exfiltration: Restrict access to SES suppression list APIs (ses:ListSuppressedDestinations) to administrative roles only
Encrypt S3 buckets used as SES receipt rule destinations and restrict bucket policies to SES service principal only
Monitor SES receipt rules for unexpected S3, SNS, or Lambda action destinations using AWS Config

services.name: Certificate Manager
services.description: Managed service for provisioning, managing, and deploying SSL/TLS certificates

threatContext.credential-theft: Private key extraction from imported certificates, ACM PCA private CA key compromise, unauthorized certificate export for impersonation attacks
threatContext.misconfiguration: Expired certificates causing service outages, wildcard certificates over-scoped for unnecessary domains, DNS validation records left publicly accessible, missing certificate transparency logging
threatContext.privilege-escalation: ACM PCA abuse to issue certificates for unauthorized domains, cross-account certificate sharing enabling trust boundary violations, rogue CA certificate issuance for internal services
threatContext.sensitive-data-exposure: Certificate details revealing internal infrastructure naming, private CA hierarchy exposure, domain enumeration via Certificate Transparency logs

misconfiguration: Enable ACM certificate expiration monitoring via CloudWatch alarms and AWS Config rules
Use ACM-managed certificates with automatic renewal instead of manually imported certificates where possible
Restrict wildcard certificate usage and prefer specific FQDN certificates to limit exposure scope
Enable Certificate Transparency logging for all public certificates to detect unauthorized issuance
credential-theft: Use ACM-managed certificates which prevent private key export rather than importing externally generated certificates
Restrict acm:ExportCertificate IAM permissions to prevent unauthorized private key retrieval for imported certificates
Protect ACM Private CA with resource-based policies restricting certificate issuance to authorized IAM principals
Enable CloudTrail logging for ACM and ACM PCA API calls to detect unauthorized certificate operations
unauthorized-access: Restrict acm:RequestCertificate and acm-pca:IssueCertificate IAM permissions to authorized roles only
Use resource-based policies on ACM Private CA to control which accounts and principals can issue certificates
Enforce aws:RequestedRegion conditions to prevent certificate provisioning in unauthorized regions
privilege-escalation: Restrict ACM PCA certificate issuance to specific certificate templates using IssueCertificate templateArn conditions
Use ACM PCA access control policies to limit certificate subject names and SANs that can be issued
Implement approval workflows for ACM PCA subordinate CA creation using SCP restrictions
sensitive-data-exposure: Use private DNS names for internal certificates to avoid revealing infrastructure details in Certificate Transparency logs
Restrict acm:DescribeCertificate and acm:ListCertificates permissions to prevent domain enumeration
Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for unauthorized certificate issuance against your domains
audit-logging-bypass: Enable CloudTrail data events for ACM and ACM PCA across all regions in the organization trail
Configure CloudWatch alarms on ACM PCA audit report generation failures
Enable ACM PCA audit reporting to S3 with Object Lock to maintain tamper-proof certificate issuance records

services.name: CloudFormation
services.description: Infrastructure as code service for modeling and provisioning AWS resources

threatContext.supply-chain-attack: Malicious CloudFormation templates from public registries or shared S3 buckets, compromised CloudFormation modules and macros, third-party resource provider backdoors, poisoned nested stack templates
threatContext.sensitive-data-exposure: Secrets hardcoded in template parameters and default values, stack outputs containing sensitive data (passwords, API keys), parameter values visible in CloudTrail and stack events, template bodies stored in S3 without encryption
threatContext.privilege-escalation: CloudFormation service role with iam:* creating admin IAM roles/policies, stack sets deploying privileged resources across accounts, custom resources executing Lambda functions with elevated permissions, StackSets administrator role abuse for organization-wide access
threatContext.injection-attack: Template parameter injection via unsanitized input in Fn::Sub and Fn::Join, custom resource request payload manipulation, macro transform code injection through CloudFormation template processing
threatContext.misconfiguration: Drift detection disabled allowing unmanaged resource changes, termination protection not enabled on critical stacks, rollback disabled allowing partially deployed insecure stacks, stack policies not configured to protect critical resources

supply-chain-attack: Validate and review all CloudFormation templates using cfn-lint and cfn_nag before deployment
Use private CloudFormation registry with approved resource types and modules instead of public third-party providers
Store templates in version-controlled repositories with code review requirements before stack operations
Pin nested stack template URLs to specific S3 object versions to prevent template substitution
sensitive-data-exposure: Use dynamic references (ssm-secure, secretsmanager) for sensitive parameters instead of plaintext defaults
Mark sensitive parameters with NoEcho to prevent values from appearing in stack events and console
Encrypt S3 buckets containing CloudFormation templates with customer-managed KMS keys
Avoid placing secrets in stack Outputs; use Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store for cross-stack secret sharing
privilege-escalation: Create dedicated CloudFormation service roles with least-privilege permissions scoped to required resource types
Use IAM permission boundaries on CloudFormation service roles to cap the maximum permissions of created resources
Restrict iam:PassRole for CloudFormation to specific approved service role ARNs
Use SCPs to restrict CloudFormation StackSets administrator role delegation to approved accounts only
misconfiguration: Enable drift detection schedules via AWS Config to identify resources modified outside CloudFormation
Enable termination protection on production stacks to prevent accidental deletion
Configure stack policies to prevent updates to critical resources (IAM roles, security groups, KMS keys)
Use CloudFormation Guard rules to validate template compliance before deployment
unauthorized-access: Restrict cloudformation:CreateStack and cloudformation:UpdateStack IAM permissions to authorized deployment roles only
Use cloudformation:TemplateUrl IAM condition key to restrict which template sources can be used
Enforce cloudformation:RoleArn condition to require specific service roles for stack operations
excessive-permissions: Scope CloudFormation service roles to only the resource types required by the stack templates
Use IAM Access Analyzer to identify and remove unused permissions on CloudFormation execution roles
Restrict StackSets administration to specific organizational units rather than the entire organization
injection-attack: Validate all template parameter inputs against AllowedPattern and AllowedValues constraints
Avoid using Fn::Sub with user-supplied input in resource properties that support code execution
Restrict CloudFormation macro creation and usage to trusted accounts using IAM policies

services.name: PrivateLink
services.description: Private connectivity to AWS services and endpoint services via interface VPC endpoints

threatContext.network-misconfiguration: Interface endpoints without a restrictive endpoint policy (default full-access policy), security groups on endpoint ENIs allowing 0.0.0.0/0, private DNS enabled without matching resolver configuration causing traffic to bypass the endpoint
threatContext.unauthorized-access: Endpoint service exposed to unintended consumers, missing endpoint policy allowing any principal/action, cross-account endpoint connection auto-accepted without review
threatContext.data-exfiltration: Attacker-created interface endpoint providing a private, Flow-Log-light path to move data to services or a rogue endpoint service in another account
threatContext.excessive-permissions: Endpoint service allowedPrincipals set to "*" or a whole account rather than specific IAM principals, permitting any AWS account to connect
threatContext.misconfiguration: Endpoint policy left as the default "allow all", acceptance of connection requests set to auto-accept, endpoint deployed without private DNS or in the wrong subnets/AZs
threatContext.lateral-movement: Cross-account PrivateLink connections used to pivot between VPCs and accounts while avoiding public network controls and inspection

network-misconfiguration: Attach a least-privilege VPC endpoint policy to every interface endpoint instead of relying on the default full-access policy
Scope the security group on endpoint ENIs to only the CIDRs and ports that require the service
Validate private DNS and Route 53 Resolver settings so traffic resolves to the endpoint rather than the public service
unauthorized-access: Restrict endpoint service allowedPrincipals to specific IAM ARNs rather than accounts or "*"
Disable auto-accept on endpoint services and manually review each connection request
Use aws:SourceVpce and aws:SourceVpc IAM conditions on downstream resources to require access via approved endpoints
data-exfiltration: Use SCPs to restrict which principals may create VPC endpoints and to approved service names only
Enable VPC Flow Logs on endpoint subnets and monitor connections to unexpected endpoint services
Apply endpoint policies that limit which resources (e.g., specific S3 buckets) are reachable through the endpoint
excessive-permissions: Set endpoint service allowedPrincipals to explicit consumer IAM principals and review the list regularly
Prefer resource-share and Organizations-scoped access over broad or wildcard principal grants
Audit endpoint service permissions with AWS Config and IAM Access Analyzer for cross-account exposure
misconfiguration: Enforce non-default endpoint policies via AWS Config rules and infrastructure-as-code review gates
Require manual acceptance of endpoint connections and deploy endpoints across the intended subnets/AZs
Use IAM Access Analyzer to detect endpoint services shared outside the organization
lateral-movement: Segment endpoint services per trust zone and avoid sharing them across unrelated accounts
Require explicit connection approval and monitor cross-account endpoint connections with CloudTrail
Combine endpoint policies with security-group segmentation to constrain what a connected consumer can reach

services.name: Transit Gateway
services.description: Hub-and-spoke interconnect for VPCs, VPNs, and on-premises networks

threatContext.network-misconfiguration: Single default route table associated with all attachments creating a flat, fully-routable network, overly broad static routes and route propagation exposing unintended VPCs, blackhole routes missing for isolated segments
threatContext.lateral-movement: Compromised VPC pivoting to every other spoke because route tables permit any-to-any connectivity, missing per-domain isolation between production and non-production attachments
threatContext.data-exfiltration: Route manipulation to steer spoke traffic through an attacker-controlled inspection VPC, egress via a shared services VPC to the internet without monitoring
threatContext.unauthorized-access: Cross-account attachments accepted without review via Resource Access Manager (RAM), rogue account attaching a VPC to the shared Transit Gateway to reach internal networks
threatContext.misconfiguration: Auto-accept shared attachments enabled, appliance-mode not enabled for stateful inspection causing asymmetric routing, all attachments in one route table instead of segmented domains
threatContext.audit-logging-bypass: Transit Gateway Flow Logs not enabled, CloudWatch/S3 flow-log delivery disabled or filtered, no monitoring of route-table changes

network-misconfiguration: Use multiple Transit Gateway route tables to segment attachments into isolated routing domains instead of one shared table
Grant least-privilege routes and disable unnecessary route propagation between spokes
Add blackhole routes to explicitly block traffic between segments that must remain isolated
lateral-movement: Implement per-environment route-table isolation (e.g., prod, non-prod, shared services) so a compromised VPC cannot reach unrelated spokes
Route east-west traffic through a centralized inspection VPC with a firewall in appliance mode
Monitor VPC and Transit Gateway Flow Logs with GuardDuty to detect cross-VPC pivoting
data-exfiltration: Restrict who can modify Transit Gateway route tables using IAM and SCPs, and alert on route changes via CloudTrail
Centralize and inspect egress through a controlled shared services VPC with logging
Enable Transit Gateway Flow Logs and monitor for unexpected inter-VPC or egress traffic volumes
unauthorized-access: Disable auto-accept for shared attachments and manually review each cross-account attachment request
Share the Transit Gateway only with specific accounts/OUs via RAM rather than the whole organization
Use SCPs to restrict which accounts may create or accept Transit Gateway attachments
misconfiguration: Enable appliance mode on attachments that route through stateful inspection to avoid asymmetric routing
Manage Transit Gateway route tables and associations as code with peer review and AWS Config drift detection
Disable auto-accept and enforce segmented route-table associations by default
audit-logging-bypass: Enable Transit Gateway Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs and S3 for all attachments
Alert on Transit Gateway route-table and association changes via CloudTrail and EventBridge
Protect flow-log destinations with S3 Object Lock and restrictive resource policies
